anp/lab-practical.intro: A lab practical asks you to name structures on a figure with the labels covered. This tool gives you that practice on real anatomy figures (OpenStax), in 83 sets that follow the course: body regions and cavities, the cell, tissues, bones, muscles, the heart, vessels, the brain and every other system. Labels for structures taught later in the course stay covered and are never asked, so a set never tests what you have not met yet.
anp/lab-practical.how: Explore shows the printed labels; tap one to read what the structure is, what it does and where the course teaches it. Study masks the labels and lets you reveal them one at a time. Quiz asks you to name a highlighted box or to point to a named structure; typed answers accept common synonyms and small spelling slips and always show the correct spelling, and a retry round brings back your misses. Practical runs timed stations with no going back, like the real exam, then reviews every station at the end.

anp/anatomy-3d.intro: A turnable 3D model of the human body, built on the BodyParts3D model, with 86 structures across eleven systems: skeletal, nervous, special senses, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, lymphatic, urinary, endocrine, reproductive and integumentary. Seeing a structure in three dimensions, next to its neighbors, is what turns a flat diagram into something you can find on a body.
anp/anatomy-3d.how: Explore: tap any structure to see its name on the model and, in Why, what it is, where it sits, its key features, related structures and the lesson that teaches it. Study hides the names until you reveal them. Quiz runs rounds of ten: name a highlighted structure, or tap the one that is named. Timed runs stations against the clock and reviews them at the end. Filter by body system or by chapter; everything outside the filter stays as a faint outline so you keep your bearings.

anp/predict.intro: Physiology questions often describe one change and ask what happens next: a vessel narrows, a pump is poisoned, oxygen runs short. This tool trains exactly that reasoning, with 377 practice cases from cells to whole-body regulation, in four levels from single steps to changes the body then compensates for.
anp/predict.how: Read the scenario, then predict for each variable whether it goes up, goes down or stays the same. Each prediction is marked on its own, so a partly right answer gets partial credit, and every variable shows the chain of causes that explains it. Show the chain draws the whole cascade as one diagram. At level 4 a case comes in two stages: the immediate change, then the state after the body compensates. Filter by chapter, topic or level; the session starts with the cases you have not yet got fully right.

anp/feedback-loops.intro: Homeostasis is taught as a loop: a stimulus is detected, a control center decides, an effector responds and the variable returns toward its set point. This tool has you build 49 of the loops the course covers, among them body temperature, blood glucose, blood pressure (baroreceptors and the renin, angiotensin and aldosterone system), ADH, blood calcium, breathing and childbirth.
anp/feedback-loops.how: Each loop has the same seven slots: stimulus, receptor, afferent pathway, control center, efferent pathway, effector and response. Fill them from shuffled cards (a few belong nowhere), by tapping or by keyboard; every slot is checked with an explanation. Then classify the loop as negative or positive feedback and predict what happens when one part fails. The finished loop is drawn as a ring, with the sensing side and the response side in their own colors.

anp/pathways.intro: Much of A&P is knowing what happens in what order: blood through the heart, the conduction system, an action potential, protein synthesis, the cardiac cycle, the steps of breathing and of oxygen delivery. This tool covers 208 of those sequences across the course.
anp/pathways.how: Every pathway can be played three ways: Order (place every step on the pathway map), Missing step (choose the step that fills the gap) and Spot the error (find the one step that is wrong). After you answer, the pathway plays step by step on the same map with the reason each step comes where it does. A first miss gets one hint and a second try; only your first check counts toward mastery.

anp/graphs.intro: Physiology is full of graphs that exams ask you to read: action potentials, the ECG, the cardiac cycle (Wiggers diagram), the pressure and volume loop, the Frank and Starling curve, pressures along the vessels, lung volumes and the spirogram, and 76 graphs in all. Each one is drawn from its numbers, with labels on the lines rather than a legend.
anp/graphs.how: Explore: drag the cursor along the graph to read every curve at that point and the phase it is in, then tap a What if condition to watch the curve move to its new position, with the explanation. Quiz asks three kinds of question: read a value off the graph, name a phase (the region is then shaded) or predict how a curve shifts (the shifted curve is then drawn). For direction questions you can answer by dragging a copy of the curve where you think it goes.

anp/calculators.intro: The physiology formulas you are expected to use, worked out with every number, every step and every unit: 89 calculators including cardiac output, stroke volume and ejection fraction, mean arterial pressure, pulse pressure, flow and resistance (and the fourth-power effect of radius), net filtration pressure in a capillary, lung volumes and capacities, the FEV1 to FVC ratio, minute and alveolar ventilation, partial pressure and oxygen content of blood.
anp/calculators.how: Calculate: change the inputs and every step of the working updates live, with reference ranges and what the result means. Practice: a problem with realistic random values; the steps stay hidden until you check your answer, then the full worked solution is shown. Practice answers count toward mastery, so a miss comes back in your review queue.

anp/word-roots.intro: Most anatomy and medical terms are built from a small set of prefixes, roots and suffixes. Learn the parts and you can work out a word you have never seen. This tool has 700 word parts, each with its meaning and the language it comes from, and 957 terms built from them.
anp/word-roots.how: Decode splits a term into its parts; give the meaning of each part, suffix first, then the meaning of the whole word. Build gives a meaning and you assemble the term from part cards (tap or keyboard, no dragging). The Part bank lists every part you have met with its origin and example terms. Choose a topic and you only get terms taught up to that point. After you answer, the term links to its glossary entry.

ochem/arrow-pusher.intro: Curved arrows are how organic chemistry describes a mechanism: each arrow moves a pair of electrons. Here the arrows have consequences. Draw them on a molecule and the tool applies them: bonds break and form, formal charges are recalculated and the product you actually made appears beside the start.
ochem/arrow-pusher.how: Pick a molecule from groups that follow the mechanisms in the order you meet them, then draw arrows from a lone pair or a bond to an atom or a bond. The tool checks every arrow against valence rules, so it can tell you when an arrow could not have happened (a carbon with five bonds, electrons coming from nowhere) even though there is no single stored answer. A hint for the expected arrows is available behind a disclosure when you want it.

ochem/resonance.intro: Resonance forms are different drawings of the same molecule, made by moving electrons and never atoms. Most practice shows you the answer to agree with; this tool has you make the move and checks whether it gives a valid resonance form or a different compound.
ochem/resonance.how: Move a lone pair or a pi bond and the tool recognizes the form you drew. Because it works out every valid form of the species itself, it can say how many you have found out of how many exist, and a nudge points to one you are actually missing. Forms are ranked as you collect them, and once you have them all it explains which contributes most, applying the standard rules in order: complete octets first, then fewest formal charges, then no like charges side by side, then negative charge on the most electronegative atom. Each rule only decides when the one above it ties.

ochem/viewer-3d.intro: A wedge and dash drawing has already chosen a viewpoint for you. Here you choose it: turn a molecule in 3D until its shape is obvious, which is the skill VSEPR questions actually test.
ochem/viewer-3d.how: Drag to rotate and zoom. Tap an atom to see its bond angles, measured from the same coordinates being drawn, so methane reads 109.5 degrees, ammonia about 107 and water about 104.5. Compare them and you can see a lone pair squeezing the bonds together instead of being told it does. View options let you show lone pairs and change the style of the model.

ochem/conformations.intro: Two places the course asks you to reason about strain, usually taught as static pictures: rotating around a single bond (Newman projections) and the cyclohexane chair. Here both move.
ochem/conformations.how: Newman: turn the front carbon and watch the energy curve follow, through the eclipsed maxima and staggered minima, with the standard energy costs (a gauche interaction about 0.9 kcal/mol) shown as you pass them. Chair: a 3D cyclohexane where axial and equatorial are worked out from the geometry; place substituents and flip the chair to see which positions swap, so the classic results (trans 1,2 and cis 1,3 can both be diequatorial) follow from the shape rather than a rule to memorize. Build your own lets you set up your own case.

ochem/reaction-predictor.intro: SN1, SN2, E1 or E2: the question Organic I turns on. It is hard because the factors argue with each other: the substrate points one way, the reagent another, and the solvent and heat lean too. This tool practices deciding between them.
ochem/reaction-predictor.how: Choose a substrate, a reagent, a solvent and the temperature, and commit to your prediction before you see the answer. The verdict comes back factor by factor: what the substrate, the nucleophile or base, the solvent and the temperature each argued for and how strongly, so you see which one overruled which. Products are given as condensed formulas. The reasoning is a decision procedure over those factors, not a table of stored answers, so any combination you set up gets an answer.

ochem/acid-base.intro: Ranking acids by structure uses a mnemonic (atom, resonance, induction, orbital); measured pKa values are the truth. This tool shows the two side by side, so you learn the mnemonic as an argument with an order of priority, not as an oracle.
ochem/acid-base.how: Pick two structures and decide which gives up its proton more easily. The answer always comes from the measured pKa. The explanation walks the factors in order and names the first one that differs. When the structural rules and the measured values disagree (ethanol against water is the classic case), the tool says so and names what the rules left out. More practice is in the Details tab.

ochem/spectroscopy.intro: Spectroscopy is taught as tables to memorize and then tested as a puzzle. This tool fills the gap between them with IR and proton NMR spectra drawn from real values: each IR band at its true wavenumber and shape, and each NMR signal split into its true number of lines.
ochem/spectroscopy.how: Three modes, the same material three ways. The reference charts let you explore a region of the spectrum instead of looking it up. The predictor takes a known compound apart peak by peak, linking every signal to the protons that make it. The puzzle runs the other way: you get a formula, an IR spectrum and an NMR spectrum, and pick the compound from four candidates, the way exams ask it.

ochem/reagent-roadmap.intro: Every functional group interconversion in the course as one map. Knowing single reactions is not the same as knowing how to get from one group to another, which is what synthesis questions ask; the notes say to learn the reactions as a map, not a list, and this is the map.
ochem/reagent-roadmap.how: Route: pick a start and a target and get the shortest routes, step by step, with the reagents and what each step needs. Reagent: pick or search a reagent and see everything it does in the course. Groups: pick a functional group to see what it becomes, what makes it and what does not work on it. Routes are searched over the reactions, not stored, and they respect substitution patterns, so the tool will not route through a step the actual molecule cannot take.

ochem/synthesis.intro: Being able to name the reagent for one step is not the same as planning a route of three. This trainer makes the plan the thing you practice: you get a starting material and a target, and build the route one step at a time.
ochem/synthesis.how: At each step choose one of four reagents and see the intermediate it makes. A choice that is real chemistry but leads nowhere is not simply marked wrong: the tool says what it made and why that is a dead end, so you can step back. Work forward from the start or backward from the target. Any route that gets there counts, and a solved problem shows the shortest route if yours was longer. The reactions come from the same map as the Reagent Roadmap.

nremt/scenario-sim.intro: The NREMT cognitive exam is built on patient scenarios: it asks what you do first, next and instead. This simulator lets you run whole EMT calls, from scene size-up through assessment, treatment and transport, where every decision changes what happens next.
nremt/scenario-sim.how: Each call starts with dispatch information. At every step you choose what to do, and the patient responds to your choice: good care stabilizes, while a missed step or a wrong priority shows up later in the call, the way it would on scene. When the call ends, the debrief goes through each decision: what you chose, what it cost, and what the best choice was and why. That makes every call practice for the scenario questions on the exam.

nremt/sound-trainer.intro: Recognizing breath and heart sounds by ear is part of patient assessment: wheezes, crackles, rhonchi, stridor and diminished breath sounds each point toward a different problem, and so do the heart sounds S1 to S4, a split S2 and murmurs by their timing. This trainer plays real recordings so you learn what each one sounds like, not just its definition.
nremt/sound-trainer.how: Start by listening to each sound with its description: where you hear it, when in the breath or heartbeat, and what it suggests (for example wheezes with narrowed lower airways, crackles with fluid in the small airways, stridor with an upper airway obstruction). Then switch to the quiz: a sound plays and you name it, and the quiz comes back more often to the sounds you keep missing. Headphones help with the quieter sounds; a phone speaker loses some of them.

nremt/body-map.intro: A real 3D model of the human body for EMT anatomy: turn it, tap a region and see the structures inside it and the assessment findings that matter there. It connects the anatomy you learn to where you would look and what you would find on a patient.
nremt/body-map.how: Drag to turn the body and tap any region or structure to read what it is and why it matters in the field, from landmarks for assessment to the organs at risk in an injury there. Quiz yourself by naming highlighted structures or finding named ones on the model. The anatomy and physiology chapter of the NREMT notes covers the same systems in text.
